vignette: Hana was sixty-two when her body first betrayed her. It began not with a dramatic collapse, but with a sudden, hollow weakness at her kitchen table, the kind that left her gripping the edge until her knuckles whitened. By the time she was wheeled into the emergency suite, she was already on a metal gurney, the cool steel pressing against her back, the sharp scent of antiseptic filling her nose. The life-threatening illness that followed demanded a cascade of medical procedures: intubation, repeated endoscopies, and multiple lines secured with needles that glinted under the hospital lights. She lay tethered to plastic drips and coiled tubing for weeks, watching the ceiling while nurses adjusted the equipment. When she was finally discharged, a quiet certainty had settled in. She had come to believe that her life had been destroyed, not by a single loss, but by the sudden derailment of her daily rhythm. She was certain that her body was no longer something she could trust, a faulty engine that could stall without warning. The months that followed were marked by a heavy, wordless weight. Hana found she could not seem to put the frightening event into words; instead, the memory returned in full sensory reliving, arriving unannounced across her senses at once. A particular conversation topic—colleagues discussing hospital stays, chronic conditions, or the quiet uncertainties of aging—would suddenly pull her forward into the room where it had happened. She would feel her body reenactment, as though her shoulders and spine were locked in the exact position they had held on the hospital gurney, her gut twisting with the ghost of those repeated procedures. What frightened her most was not the physical discomfort, but the shame that crept in with the recollection. She felt ashamed of what happened to her body, of the visible marks left by tubes and the way her frame seemed to shrink under the weight of medical attention. Her PCL5 score of 62 mirrored this steady accumulation rather than a sudden decline, reflecting how the symptoms occupied her days without overtaking them entirely. At work, where she coordinated cross-departmental project timelines as a project manager, Hana encountered the visual triggers of her trauma with particular frequency. A junior analyst’s IV drip during a wellness presentation made her register the flinch; the glint of a lavalier microphone clipped to a lapel reminded her of the metal clips used in her own procedure. Her avoidance formed gradually, a series of quiet retreats that accumulated over weeks and months. She began steering clear of routine medical examinations, postponing check-ups until they became urgent. She stopped attending the quarterly health seminars, chose parking spaces closer to clinic exits, and let the doctor’s visits slide until her husband gently reminded her. These habits did not stem from one another but simply coexisted in her life, each making sense in the moment. She had come to dread certain conversation topics and medical procedures not because they caused her distress, but because they echoed the very uncertainties that had hospitalized her. Alongside the retreats, her threat responses surfaced in the everyday. She found herself irritable, prone to angry outbursts when the quiet routine of her home was disrupted by unexpected noise or routine requests. Her concentration suffered; during project team meetings, she would lose the thread of a presentation, her mind drifting back to the hum of equipment and the cold press of medical gear. Startle to touch became a daily reality. When her husband reached to brush a strand of hair from her face, or when a colleague lightly touched her arm during a debrief, she would react with alarm, her breath catching as if anticipating another intervention. These responses simply existed together, each occupying its own space in her daily experience. She was certain that another medical episode was always possible, and her body’s unreliability meant she could not afford to let her guard down. Now, at sixty-three, Hana sits at her kitchen table much as she did the day everything shifted, but the silence has grown heavy. She has come to seek help not because her condition worsened, but because the quiet dread had solidified into a steady daily burden. She is most afraid of the moment her body will fail her again without warning, of the slow, unspoken erosion of her married life and her work. What she hopes for is not a return to exactly how things were, but a steady trust in her own frame, a life that no longer waits for the other shoe to drop.
